'''Narayana polynomials''' are a class of polynomials whose coefficients are the [[Narayana numbers]]. The Narayana numbers and Narayana polynomials are named after the Canadian mathematician [[Tadepalli Venkata Narayana|T. V. Narayana]] (1930–1987). They appear in several combinatorial problems.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=D. G. Rogers |title=Rhyming schemes: Crossings and coverings |journal=Discrete Mathematics |date=1981 |volume=33 |pages=67–77 |doi=10.1016/0012-365X(81)90259-4 |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82236401.pdf |access-date=2 December 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=R.P. Stanley |title=Enumerative Combinatorics, Vol. 2 |date=1999 |publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rodica Simian and Daniel Ullman |title=On the structure of the lattice of noncrossing partitions |journal=Discrete Mathematics |date=1991 |volume=98 |issue=3 |pages=193–206 |doi=10.1016/0012-365X(91)90376-D |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82065542.pdf |access-date=2 December 2023}}</ref>

==Definitions==

For a positive integer <math>n</math> and for an integer <math>k\geq0</math>, the Narayana number <math>N(n,k)</math>  is defined by
:<math> N(n,k) = \frac{1}{n}{n \choose k}{n\choose k-1}.</math>
The number <math>N(0,k)</math> is defined as <math>1</math> for <math>k=0</math> and as <math>0</math> for <math>k\ne0</math>. 

For a nonnegative integer <math>n </math>, the <math>n</math>-th Narayana polynomial <math>N_n(z)</math> is defined by
:<math>N_n(z) = \sum_{k=0}^n N(n,k)z^k.</math>

The associated Narayana polynomial <math>\mathcal N_n(z)</math> is defined as the [[reciprocal polynomial]] of <math>N_n(z)</math>:
:<math>\mathcal N_n(z)=z^nN_n\left(\tfrac{1}{z}\right)</math>.

==Examples==

The first few Narayana polynomials are 
:<math>N_0(z)=1</math>
:<math>N_1(z)=z</math>
:<math>N_2(z)=z^2+z </math>
:<math>N_3(z)=z^3+3z^2+z </math>
:<math>N_4(z)=z^4+6z^3+6z^2+z </math>
:<math>N_5(z)=z^5+10z^4+20z^3+10z^2+z </math>

==Properties==
A few of the properties of the Narayana polynomials and the associated Narayana polynomials are collected below. Further information on the properties of these polynomials are available in the references cited.

=== Alternative form of the Narayana polynomials ===

The Narayana polynomials can be expressed in the following alternative form:<ref name="Chen">{{cite arXiv |last1=Ricky X. F. Chen and Christian M. Reidys |title=Narayana polynomials and some generalizations |date=2014 |class=math.CO |eprint=1411.2530 }}</ref>
*<math>N_n(z)= \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{1}{n+1}{n+1 \choose k}{2n-k \choose n}(z-1)^k </math>

=== Special values ===

* <math>N_n(1) </math> is the <math>n</math>-th [[Catalan number]] <math>C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}{2n \choose n} </math>. The first few Catalan numbers are <math>1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429, \ldots</math>. {{OEIS|id=A000108}}.<ref name="Sun">{{cite arXiv |last1=Toufik Mansour, Yidong Sun |title=Identities involving Narayana polynomials and Catalan numbers |date=2008 |class=math.CO |eprint=0805.1274 }}</ref>
* <math>N_n(2) </math> is the <math>n</math>-th large [[Schröder number]]. This is the number of plane trees having <math>n</math> edges with leaves colored by one of two colors. The first few Schröder numbers are <math>1, 2, 6, 22, 90, 394, 1806, 8558, \ldots</math>. {{OEIS|id=A006318}}.<ref name="Sun"/>
*For integers <math>n\ge 0</math>, let <math>d_n</math> denote the number of underdiagonal paths from <math>(0,0)</math> to <math>(n,n)</math> in a <math>n\times n</math> grid having step set <math>S = \{(k, 0) : k \in \mathbb N^+\} \cup \{(0, k) : k \in \mathbb N^+\}</math>. Then <math>d_n = \mathcal N(4)</math>.<ref name="Coker">{{cite journal |last1=Curtis Coker |title=Enumerating a class oflattice paths |journal=Discrete Mathematics |date=2003 |volume=271 |issue=1–3 |pages=13–28 |doi=10.1016/S0012-365X(03)00037-2 |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82292598.pdf |access-date=1 December 2023}}</ref>

=== Recurrence relations ===

*For <math>n \ge 3</math>, <math>\mathcal N_n(z)</math> satisfies the following nonlinear recurrence relation:<ref name="Coker"/>
:<math>\mathcal N_n(z) = (1+z)N_{n-1}(z) + z \sum_{k=1}^{n-2}\mathcal N_k(z)\mathcal N_{n-k-1}(z)</math>.
*For <math>n\ge 3</math>, <math>\mathcal N_n(z)</math> satisfies the following second order linear recurrence relation:<ref name="Coker"/>
:<math>(n+1)\mathcal N_n(z) = (2n-1)(1+z)\mathcal N_{n-1}(z) - (n-2)(z-1)^2\mathcal N_{n-2}(z)</math> with <math>\mathcal N_1(z)=1</math> and <math>\mathcal N_2(z)=1+z</math>.

=== Generating function ===

The ordinary [[generating function]] the Narayana polynomials is given by
: <math> \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} N_n(z)t^n = \frac{1+t-t z -\sqrt{1 - 2(1+z) t + (1-z)^2 t^2 }}{2 t}.</math>

=== Integral representation ===

The <math>n</math>-th degree [[Legendre polynomial]] <math>P_n(x)</math> is given by
:<math> P_n(x) = 2^{-n}\sum_{k=0}^{\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor } (-1)^k {n-k \choose k}{2n-2k \choose n-k}x^{n-2k}</math>
Then, for ''n'' > 0, the Narayana polynomial <math>N_n(z)</math> can be expressed in the following form:
*<math>N_n(z)=(z-1)^{n+1}\int_0^{\frac{z}{z-1}} P_n(2x-1)\,dx</math>.
